title: Builder and ExecutionContext
sub: How the task learns about an exception, and what travels across await
cards/0/title: The exception goes into the task
cards/0/body:
The generated MoveNext is wrapped in try/catch. If an exception is thrown inside, the catch doesn't rethrow it but calls builder.SetException(ex), and the task moves to the Faulted state. The exception "rides" inside the task until someone awaits it: await (that is, GetResult) throws it again.

A consequence: even an exception before the first await doesn't escape the call of a Task-returning method. The first MoveNext runs inside the call, but its catch still puts the exception into the task.
cards/1/q: Inside an async Task method, an exception is thrown after an await. What does the generated code do with it?
cards/1/options/0: Calls builder.SetException: the task becomes Faulted and await will throw the exception
cards/1/options/1: Throws it on the thread that ran the continuation and crashes the process
cards/1/options/2: Swallows it: the task completes successfully
cards/1/explain: The catch in MoveNext hands the exception to the builder, and it waits in the task for whoever awaits it.
cards/2/q: var t = ParseAsync(""); — the method throws ArgumentException before its first await. What does the caller get on this line?
cards/2/options/0: A task in the Faulted state; the exception is thrown at await t
cards/2/options/1: The exception, right on this line
cards/2/explain: The first MoveNext runs synchronously, but its catch calls SetException. An exception never escapes the call of an async Task method.
cards/3/body: Along with the continuation, .NET carries the ExecutionContext: the current culture, AsyncLocal<T> values and other "ambient" data of the operation. The context is captured at the pause and restored before the continuation runs, on whatever thread that is. That's why AsyncLocal is visible after await even when another thread runs the continuation.
cards/4/q: What does Log print after the await?
cards/4/options/2: It depends on which thread runs the continuation
cards/4/explain: ExecutionContext carried the AsyncLocal value along with the continuation, so the thread doesn't matter.
cards/5/body: A [ThreadStatic] field belongs to a thread, not to an operation. If another thread continues the code after await, you read that thread's value. It's either null or, worse, the value of another request that ran on this pool thread earlier. For per-request or per-operation data, use AsyncLocal.
cards/5/deep: A change to AsyncLocal inside a called async method isn't visible to the caller after it returns: ExecutionContext is immutable and copied on write. The value flows down the call chain, not up.
cards/6/q: An ASP.NET Core server. At the start of a request a [ThreadStatic] field is set: _user = "ann". Then comes an await on a database query, then Log(_user). What can Log print?
cards/6/options/0: Any of the three: ann, null or another request's user name, depending on which pool thread resumes
cards/6/options/1: Always ann: the value was written in this same request
cards/6/options/2: Always null: the field is cleared after await
cards/6/explain: Any pool thread may run the continuation, and [ThreadStatic] holds whatever that thread's last user wrote into it.
cards/7/q: What travels across await with the ExecutionContext? Select all that apply.
cards/7/explain: ThreadStatic and the thread number belong to the thread, not the operation, so they don't travel across await.
cards/8/pairs/0/1: Creates and completes the method's task
cards/8/pairs/2/1: A container of ambient data carried across await
cards/8/pairs/3/1: A single value tied to a logical operation
cards/8/pairs/4/1: Per-thread data, lost when the thread changes
